strengths: The proposed GradPower transformation is extremely simple (one line of code, no changes to base optimizer internals or hyperparameters), and the paper convincingly demonstrates a negligible wall-clock overhead (0.4%).

The empirical evaluation is broad and unusually thorough for an optimizer paper: LLaMA (66M–2B) and Qwen2MoE (0.5B–2B), C4 and OpenWebText, both cosine and wsd schedules, downstream zero-shot benchmarks, compatibility with Muon and Blockwise LR, ablations over clipping order, β1/β2 sweeps, and multi-seed runs with standard deviations (Appendix B.4).

The paper is transparent about closely related prior work: Appendix A honestly acknowledges that the Powerball method (Yuan et al., 2019) uses essentially the same sign-power transformation, and clearly delineates the differences (modern adaptive optimizers, LLM pre-training, both p<1 and p>1 regimes, batch-size-dependent theory).

The theoretical section is well-aligned with experiments: the 1D uniform-noise example (Example 5.1) predicts that the optimal power p* exceeds 1 in the high-noise regime and falls below 1 at large batch sizes, which matches both the p=1.2 default and the batch-size ablation in Figure 6 (right); convergence results for AdagradPower in low- and high-noise regimes are provided with full proofs.
The batch-size study (Section 4.6) connecting the optimal p to gradient noise levels provides a useful, testable insight and links theory to practice.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited: the core transformation |g|^p sign(g) is essentially the Powerball method from 2019, and Powerpropagation uses the same functional form. The contribution is primarily the application to modern LLM pre-training at scale plus the batch-size/p analysis, which is incremental rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The theoretical guarantees are proved only for Adagrad (AdagradPower), not for AdamW, which is the optimizer actually used in all experiments. The claimed acceleration comparisons are also somewhat non-standard (comparing E||∇L||^{p+1} metrics against the classical ||∇L||^2 rate), so the '2/(p+1)× faster' claim should be interpreted cautiously.

The mechanistic story connecting GradPower to amplifying 'flat/river' directions (Section 3, contributions bullet 3) remains largely intuitive; the paper's own flat-direction terminology is admittedly approximate, and the MoE stability and wsd benefits are left as hypotheses for future work.

While p=1.2 is claimed to be robust, it is still an additional hyperparameter, and the batch-size study shows the optimal p can drop below 1 for large batches, meaning the 'no extra tuning' claim holds only within the standard small-batch regime.

The theoretical Assumptions 5.6 and 5.9 are strong per-coordinate conditions (E[g_i^p]∇_iL ≥ c|∇_iL|^{p+1}, etc.) whose satisfaction in realistic LLM training is argued only indirectly; direct empirical verification of these assumptions is absent.

Absolute loss improvements are modest in some settings (e.g., ~0.015–0.03 for dense models), and multi-seed statistical validation is provided only for a small subset of the experiments; no public code release is mentioned, which slightly weakens reproducibility despite detailed configuration tables in the appendix.

strengths: The proposed method is extremely simple and cheap: a single elementwise sign-power transform applied before a base optimizer, with measured wall-clock overhead of only ~0.4% (Section 4.1), which is a genuinely practical selling point.

The empirical evaluation is broad and largely well-controlled: LLaMA (66M–2B) and Qwen2MoE (0.5B–2B), C4 and OpenWebText, cos and wsd schedules, tuned AdamW baselines via an lr grid (Tables 3–4), compatibility tests with Blockwise LR and Muon, a batch-size study (Section 4.6), multi-seed reruns for a subset (Appendix B.4), and a (β1, β2) robustness sweep (Appendix B.5) showing AdamWPower still beats the best tuned AdamW.

The batch-size experiment (Figure 6 right, Table 2) and the 1D toy analysis (Example 5.1, Figure 7) form a coherent, testable story: the optimal power p decreases as gradient noise decreases, and the paper honestly flags the 'flat directions' terminology mismatch with classical Hessian-based flatness (Section 2/3).

Appendix A transparently situates the work relative to the Powerball method (Yuan et al., 2019) and Powerpropagation (Schwarz et al., 2021), and the proofs in Appendices C–D are complete and mostly careful.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core method. The central technique — transforming gradients by sign(g)|g|^p before the optimizer — is essentially the Powerball method (Yuan et al., 2019), as the authors themselves admit ('shares the similar methodology as our approach') in Appendix A, yet this is relegated to the appendix and framed as discovered 'after completing this work'. The main text presents GradPower as a new approach. The remaining contribution is applying a known transformation to AdamW/Muon at LLM scale plus new theory, which is incremental.

The theoretical results do not support the claimed 'strict acceleration'. Theorem 5.8 bounds E||∇L||^{p+1}_{p+1} for AdagradPower and compares against an O(T^{-(p+1)/4}) rate derived from Theorem 5.5 for the norm ||∇L||^2_2. These are different convergence metrics, so the '2/(p+1)× faster' claim is not an apples-to-apples comparison; by the same logic any convergent method 'accelerates' under a reweighted norm. Theorem 5.11's high-noise gain is only a constant factor R^{p−1}/σ. Moreover, the theory is for Adagrad while all experiments use AdamW/Muon, leaving a substantial theory–practice gap the paper glosses over.

The assumptions underpinning the theorems are strong and partly do the work of the conclusions. Assumption 5.6/5.9 impose coordinate-wise moment conditions E[g_i^p]∇_iL ≥ c|∇_iL|^{p+1} (or ≥ σ|∇iL|²) that hold only for narrowly specified distributions (deterministic, uniform, binary — Examples 5.7/5.10); there is no evidence these hold, even approximately, in LLM pre-training. The 'p* = 1.2 matches the empirically optimal p' claim from Example 5.1 is also weak: p* = Θ(log(ϵ log(1/σ))/log σ) depends sensitively on ϵ and σ, so the coincidence with 1.2 appears fortuitous rather than predictive.

The empirical gains are modest and the downstream evidence is mixed. Terminal-loss improvements are typically ~0.01–0.05 nats, the downstream evaluation (Table 1) shows AdamWPower losing on ARC-C (26.28 vs 26.45), and multi-seed error bars are provided only for two small-model settings (Appendix B.4) rather than the headline 1B/2B results where spike behavior is claimed to improve. The claimed MoE stability benefit is explicitly only a 'hypothesis' (Section 4.3).

Presentation and citation quality issues. The main text's related-work framing ('we propose a lightweight, plug-in approach by revisiting the core component') understates the direct precedent; several citations are future-dated or obscure (Orvieto & Gower, 2026, 'NeurIPS 38'; Wang et al., 2026, arXiv:2602.14208; Zhu et al., 2026, arXiv:2602.22681), and Appendix D contains unfinished prose ('This generalize is not trivial, need to use the structure of the high-noise fact'). Lemma D.1 is stated 'for any σ > 0' but is applied with σ = c in a low-noise argument where the roles of σ and c differ, which deserves clarification.

Limitations are not systematically discussed: there is no section acknowledging that (i) the method is a rediscovery, (ii) theory covers only Adagrad, and (iii) the mechanism for MoE/wsd benefits remains unexplained; these caveats appear only scattered in the text.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation covering a genuinely broad pre-training landscape: dense LLaMA (66M–2B) and Qwen2MoE architectures, C4 and OpenWebText, cosine and wsd schedules, downstream zero-shot benchmarks, and compatibility with Muon and Blockwise LR, which substantiates the central claim of consistent terminal-loss improvement.

The method's practicality is convincingly demonstrated: a single-line code change, no modification to base optimizer internals or hyperparameters, a measured wall-clock overhead of only ~0.4%, and a single small-scale tuning of p=1.2 that transfers across models, datasets, and architectures.

Good empirical hygiene: multi-seed reruns with standard deviations (Appendix B.4), robustness sweeps over (β1, β2) showing the advantage persists after tuning momentum parameters, a controlled study of clipping order, and an instructive batch-size study linking optimal p to noise level.

The paper provides a mechanistic explanation connecting the batch-size dependence of the optimal exponent p to a noise-to-signal analysis, with a clean 1D closed-form study (Propositions 5.2–5.3) whose predicted optimal power matches the empirically used p=1.2 in the high-noise regime.

The discussion of 'flat directions' terminology, its approximation relative to Hessian-based notions, and the acknowledged noise-dominated-regime assumption is unusually careful and honest, and the limitations/future-work discussion is appropriate.
weaknesses: Limited originality of the core idea: the sign-power gradient transformation φp(g)=|g|^p sign(g) is essentially identical to the Powerball method (Yuan et al., 2019), which the authors only discovered after completing the work and relegate to Appendix A. While the LLM pre-training setting, p>1 regime, and theory are new, the central mechanism is not, and this overlap should be treated as a first-class contribution caveat rather than an appendix note.

The theoretical guarantees are for Adagrad, not Adam or Muon, and the headline 'strict acceleration' claim is weaker than it appears: Theorem 5.8 measures a nonstandard quantity ‖∇L‖_{p+1}^{p+1}, and the claimed 2/(p+1)× speedup is obtained by comparison against a Jensen-relaxed rate in a different metric. The assumptions in 5.6/5.9 (per-coordinate moment conditions on the stochastic gradient relative to the full-batch gradient) largely encode the desired regime into the assumptions. The connection to the actual AdamWPower experiments remains heuristic.

The empirical gains, while consistent, are modest in absolute terms (terminal-loss improvements of ~0.015–0.045), and the 'favorable scaling laws' claim should be interpreted cautiously: in Figure 1 the curves appear nearly parallel, indicating a roughly constant FLOPs-equivalent advantage rather than an improving scaling exponent.

The strongest baselines are AdamW and Muon; comparisons against other strong recent LLM optimizers (e.g., Lion, AdEMAMix, Sophia, SOAP) are absent, so it is unclear where AdamWPower would rank in the broader optimizer landscape, and whether reported gains would persist against these.

Statistical support is uneven: multi-seed experiments cover only a subset of settings (66M and 0.2B on C4, cos), while the headline 1B/2B and MoE results, where the claimed stability benefits appear, appear to be single-seed; loss-spike reduction claims are labeled a hypothesis without targeted analysis.

Presentation has rough edges: proof sketches contain typos and imprecise language ('Adamgradpower', 'This generalize is not trivial'), and no explicit code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility despite detailed appendix configurations.

The batch-size study (Section 4.6) uses a single model size (0.2B, wsd) and evaluates only p in [0.8, 1.4], leaving the predicted regime p*<1 at large batch only weakly verified; similarly, the MoE/wsd advantages are observed but left unexplained, as the authors themselves acknowledge.
